summary: This memo lists books related to using the Internet, as of 1993. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This paper is a reading list of books about how to use the Internet, from the early days when there were few of them.

subtitle: A guide to books about the Internet and its networks as of 1993.

tldr.problem: As the Internet grew in the early 1990s, many new books appeared to help people understand and use it, but there was no comprehensive list to guide readers.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC collects and categorizes about 26 Internet books of the era, describing each one with publication details, prices, and intended audiences.
tldr.outcome: This snapshot from 1993 documents the state of Internet literature when the network was young and still mostly unknown to the general public.

today: RFC 1432 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted. It remains a historical snapshot of Internet literature from the early 1990s, useful for understanding what information was available to users when the Internet was still young and largely unknown.

sections.title: Overview of Internet Books
sections.content: In 1993, the Internet was growing rapidly yet remained unknown to most people. The RFC notes nine or ten new books on the Internet had recently been published, along with older titles going back to 1984. The books covered many topics: some focused entirely on the Internet, while others addressed broader networks like the Matrix (the global collection of interconnected computer networks including FidoNet, UUCP, BITNET, USENET, and the Internet). This collection focuses on Internet-related books because of the recent surge in publications about it.
sections.plainLanguage: In 1993, lots of new books came out about the Internet because more people wanted to learn about it. This paper lists the books and tells who they are for.

sections.title: Categories of Internet Books
sections.content: The RFC groups the books into categories based on their approach and audience. Introductions include new user guides aimed at the general public and technical audiences, ranging from LaQuey and Ryer's beginner guide at $10.95 to more comprehensive references like Krol's user's guide and resource catalog. A separate Travelogs category contains Malamud's humorous technical exploration. Standards books examine how Internet standards are created, including works on UNIX, POSIX, and open systems. Textbooks for librarians and information professionals address instruction and policy. A Hacking and Cracking section covers computer security history, differentiating between skillful hackers and network criminals. Resource Guides provide reference materials for users, while the final category covers books about other networks including the broader Matrix of computer networks worldwide.
sections.plainLanguage: The books are organized by what they teach: how to use the Internet, funny stories about it, how standards are made, how to teach others, hacker history, reference guides, and books about networks besides the Internet.

sections.title: Notable Books and Trends
sections.content: Several books stand out in the 1993 landscape. LaQuey and Ryer's Internet Companion was the least expensive entry point, also available online via FTP. Krol's The Whole Internet User's Guide and Catalog was the most ambitious of the new books, combining user guidance with a resource catalog aimed at researchers. Malamud's Exploring the Internet offered a technical travelogue with accurate background and humor. For those interested in Internet standards, Quarterman and Wilhelm's book provided context about open systems standards and the IETF standards process. Stoll's The Cuckoo's Egg brought network security to popular audiences through a true spy story. The collection demonstrates that by 1993, the Internet was important enough to warrant substantial publishing investment across multiple genres and audiences.
sections.plainLanguage: Some books were cheap and simple for beginners. Others were long and detailed for people doing research. Some told funny or exciting stories about the Internet. Different books worked best for different kinds of readers.

sections.title: Accessing the Books
sections.content: The RFC provides extensive publication information: author names, page counts ranging from 86 to 822 pages, prices from $4.95 to $50, publishers' contact information, and telephone and fax numbers for ordering. Some books were available online via anonymous FTP, a significant development in the pre-web era. The RFC notes that prices may change, and disclaims accuracy with the warning that information was current as of publication. Contact addresses for corrections and updates are provided, reflecting an era when printed RFCs were a primary means of sharing reference information. The inclusion of email addresses, FTP locations, and publishing details demonstrates how the RFC served as a practical reference guide for users wanting to learn about and purchase these books.
sections.plainLanguage: The paper tells you how to find and buy the books, including their prices, publishers, phone numbers, and some books that were available online at the time.

sections.title: The Internet in 1993
sections.content: This RFC documents the Internet at a turning point. The network is described as the global system of more than a million computers using TCP/IP protocols, used by millions of people. The existence of a dozen or more new books reflects growing public interest and the network's transition from academic and research use toward broader adoption. Yet the books' range and difficulty levels show the Internet remained largely mysterious to outsiders: some books targeted the curious general public, others assumed technical expertise. By 1993, the World Wide Web existed but was not yet dominant, Gopher was actively used, and FTP was the primary file transfer mechanism. This RFC captures the moment when the Internet was becoming important enough for commercial publishing but before the web revolutionized how people accessed information online.
sections.plainLanguage: By 1993, over a million computers were connected to the Internet, and lots of people wanted to learn about it. This paper shows what books were available and who they were meant for.
